question_text: Assess the effectiveness of the options available to organic and biodynamic grape growers to control pests and diseases.
command_word_demand: "Far too many papers described, but did not assess the options as the paper requires." The examiners state the verb demanded analysis of trade-offs, not enumeration: "The question required the use of analytical skills to address fundamental decisions vital to grape growers with more limited resources relative to conventional growers."

definitions_required.quote: Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications.

required_elements.element: Define 'effectiveness', explicitly including the economic/financial implications of each control option
required_elements.quote: Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications.

required_elements.element: Assess (weigh up) the options rather than describe them
required_elements.quote: Far too many papers described, but did not assess the options as the paper requires.

required_elements.element: Distinguish organic from biodynamic conceptually (containment vs prevention)
required_elements.quote: Nor were there many papers that clearly understood the conceptual differences between organic and biodynamic options (containment vs. prevention).

required_elements.element: Make examples clearly attributable to organic OR biodynamic practice, not blurred together
required_elements.quote: In too many instances, examples did not distinguish between organic and biodynamic.

required_elements.element: Frame the analysis around the fundamental decisions facing growers with more limited resources than conventional growers
required_elements.quote: The question required the use of analytical skills to address fundamental decisions vital to grape growers with more limited resources relative to conventional growers.

required_elements.element: Cover control through canopy management, not only sprays and predator habitat

penalty_signals.signal: Presenting mainstream sustainable/conventional techniques as uniquely organic
penalty_signals.quote: Some papers treated some means of control as uniquely organic, such as pheromone usage and raptor control, when in fact these are now standard practices under sustainable and even many conventional growing systems.

penalty_signals.signal: No definition of 'effectiveness', so no yardstick against which to assess
penalty_signals.quote: Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications.

penalty_signals.signal: Omitting canopy management as a control lever

performance_note: "This question was answered by only one third of the candidates, and overall, not very successfully."
extraction_notes: The items in named_in_report are control TECHNIQUES the commentary names, not places or producers — the report names no regional or producer examples for this question. Note that 'pheromone usage' and 'raptor control' are named only to be criticised as NOT uniquely organic; a grader should not credit them as organic-specific. Paper-level preamble (Joel Butler MW) also applies: papers failed by not providing definitions where required, not answering both parts, factual inaccuracy, and answering "too generally and with inadequate generic examples"; "Reciting arguments from viticulture textbooks, while perhaps correct, will not suffice."

extraction_notes: Musar, Beaucastel and Grange are deliberately NOT in named_in_report: the report names them only as over-used and dated, so a grader must not treat citing them as a credit signal. The commentary opens with a 'Key Understanding' block (the examiners' pre-stated expectation) followed by post-hoc performance commentary; both are report text and both were mined. A page number ('the key 9 purveyors') was removed from one quote.

question_text: Shape, size and material of a vessel used for fermentation and maturation are important factors in determining style and quality. Discuss with particular reference to Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay.
command_word_demand: Discussion here meant causal analysis, not a survey of practice: "Candidates should not merely have discussed who does what but should have analysed the important factors that determine quality and style." And: "Strong answers must address the physical dynamics of why certain shapes / sizes / materials have a material effect upon end flavours."

required_elements.element: Address BOTH named varieties — declining one forfeits marks
required_elements.quote: Many candidates asserted their right to speak only of either Chardonnay or Cabernet Sauvignon and consequently limited their scope for gaining marks… when the question specifies the varietal commentary required, it is not sufficient for a candidate to state in their introduction that they do not intend to address one or other of the named varieties.

required_elements.element: Discuss both fermentation and maturation
required_elements.quote: They must discuss both fermentation and maturation.

required_elements.element: Explain the physical dynamics by which shape/size/material change the end flavour
required_elements.quote: Strong answers must address the physical dynamics of why certain shapes / sizes / materials have a material effect upon end flavours.

required_elements.element: Show that some of these choices are highly grape-variety specific
required_elements.quote: They should make it clear that these choices are sometimes highly grape variety specific.

required_elements.element: Show global breadth of styles and qualities from both varieties, across classic and non-classic origins
required_elements.quote: Candidates must be able to show depth and breadth of knowledge about which styles and qualities are produced from these two varieties globally and consider styles with reference to classic / non classic origins.

required_elements.element: Analyse the determinants of style and quality rather than catalogue who does what
required_elements.quote: Candidates should not merely have discussed who does what but should have analysed the important factors that determine quality and style.

required_elements.element: Cover the full market, not only premium wines
required_elements.quote: Again, Examiners noted that candidates focussed too heavily on the premium end of the market. The best candidates covered the use of various vessels for both wine types and a range of styles.

credit_signals.signal: Grasping the full range of options while staying practically realistic
credit_signals.quote: Candidates that performed well grasped the dimensions of possibility whilst maintaining a grip upon practicality.

credit_signals.signal: Acknowledging excellent wines made in unfashionable vessels
credit_signals.quote: They also tended to acknowledge the fact that there are many wineries making excellent wines from vessels and materials that are not currently in vogue - so a palpable sense of practical realism helped strengthen their arguments.

credit_signals.signal: Presenting a clear spectrum of causes and effects
credit_signals.quote: Recognition of the fact that different vessel materials and shapes and sizes do make significant differences to wine style was crucial and the best papers presented a spectrum of clearly stated causes and effects.

credit_signals.signal: Covering various vessels across both varieties and a range of styles
credit_signals.quote: The best candidates covered the use of various vessels for both wine types and a range of styles.

penalty_signals.signal: Declaring in the introduction that only one of the two named varieties will be covered
penalty_signals.quote: It is sometimes said that the candidate has the right to control the content of the essay, but when the question specifies the varietal commentary required, it is not sufficient for a candidate to state in their introduction that they do not intend to address one or other of the named varieties.

penalty_signals.signal: An 'all I know about oak' brain-dump untethered from the two varieties
penalty_signals.quote: Examiners also commented that the responses were too frequently a dump of 'all I know about oak' without giving particular reference to Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon.

penalty_signals.signal: Premium-end bias
penalty_signals.quote: Again, Examiners noted that candidates focussed too heavily on the premium end of the market.

examples_expected.specificity: Global, spanning classic and non-classic origins for both varieties and a range of price points; per the Panel Chair, "Examples should be used to support arguments/statements rather than as statements of fact. Examples should also be global and cover all wine types where appropriate."
examples_expected.quote: Candidates must be able to show depth and breadth of knowledge about which styles and qualities are produced from these two varieties globally and consider styles with reference to classic / non classic origins.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as being about oak barrels alone
scope_traps.quote: the responses were too frequently a dump of 'all I know about oak' without giving particular reference to Chardonnay and Cabernet Sauvignon.

scope_traps.trap: Answering on one named variety only
scope_traps.quote: Many candidates asserted their right to speak only of either Chardonnay or Cabernet Sauvignon and consequently limited their scope for gaining marks.

performance_note: "This question was generally better answered than most others."
extraction_notes: The commentary names no specific producers or regions for this question, so named_in_report is empty; the requirement for global/classic-vs-non-classic breadth is stated abstractly. The examples_expected specificity field draws partly on the Paper 2 preamble (Meg Brodtmann MW), which is paper-wide evidence.

question_text: How can a wine's tannin profile be managed during vinification?
command_word_demand: The examiners emphasise the scope-limiting phrase in the stem and the need to convert technical detail into argument: "The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process." And: "The less successful scripts tended to either offer 'all I know about tannin', in rather chatty style, or provided a lot of technical detail about the subject but were unable to interpret that detail into a sensible argument."

required_elements.element: Stay within vinification — viticulture/harvest gets a brief mention at most
required_elements.quote: The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process. A brief mention of harvesting grapes at optimum phenolic ripeness is fine but candidates must focus on the winemaking.

required_elements.element: Demonstrate the tannin extraction processes and the aids used to extract, add and/or fix tannins, plus oak tannins
required_elements.quote: Candidates must demonstrate an understanding of the tannin extraction processes, the use of aids to extract, add and / or fix tannins and the use of oak tannins.

required_elements.element: Focus on red winemaking while noting white, sparkling, sweet and fortified where relevant
required_elements.quote: Mention could be made of white, sparkling, sweet and fortified wine but should focus on red winemaking.

required_elements.element: Clear command of cap management techniques — how they differ and why each is used
required_elements.quote: In relation to the extraction process, candidates should have a clear understanding of the various cap management techniques, how they differ and why they are used.

required_elements.element: Cover post-fermentation operations: post-ferment maceration, microoxygenation, barrel ageing
required_elements.quote: They should have also included some discussion of post fermentation maceration and other post fermentation operations that can manage tannin (ie microoxygenation, ageing in barrels, etc).

required_elements.element: Explain pressing with authority — press fractions and fining of press fractions and free run
required_elements.quote: For those that covered pressing, few really explained with any level of authority the way tannin can be managed in a press through fractions - fining pressing fractions (and free run) is an important way of managing tannin.

required_elements.element: Address entry-level as well as premium wine
required_elements.quote: Candidates must not just focus on the premium end of the market - it could be argued that judicial tannin management is more important at "entry level" - pressing off skins before the end of primary fermentation is common practice.

required_elements.element: Structure the answer as a logical flow through the winemaking process, opened by a solid introduction
required_elements.quote: With these types of questions a logical flow to the answer helps immensely. As winemaking is itself a flow from one activity to another, it makes sense that answers cover the winemaking process in a coherent way. A solid introduction alluding to the points that will be discussed is important.

required_elements.element: Include oenological tannins — colour stabilisation, structural improvement of early-pressed wines
required_elements.quote: Many candidates, even the better ones, tended to overlook the use of oenological tannins in winemaking. Points raised could have been in connection with stabilising the colour with tannin or improving structural elements of early-pressed wines.

required_elements.element: Microoxygenation may be discussed
required_elements.quote: Candidates could also discuss microoxygenation.

credit_signals.signal: A coherent chronological flow through the winemaking process, signposted by the introduction
credit_signals.quote: With these types of questions a logical flow to the answer helps immensely… A solid introduction alluding to the points that will be discussed is important.

penalty_signals.signal: 'All I know about tannin' in a chatty register
penalty_signals.quote: The less successful scripts tended to either offer 'all I know about tannin', in rather chatty style…

penalty_signals.signal: Technical detail that is never converted into an argument
penalty_signals.quote: or provided a lot of technical detail about the subject but were unable to interpret that detail into a sensible argument.

penalty_signals.signal: Over-weighting fermentation and leaving the rest of the process thin
penalty_signals.quote: Many candidates tended to focus too much on fermentation and not give a full answer.

penalty_signals.signal: Overlooking oenological tannins
penalty_signals.quote: Many candidates, even the better ones, tended to overlook the use of oenological tannins in winemaking.

penalty_signals.signal: Disparaging particular winemaking methods
penalty_signals.quote: Lastly, as a caution, be very wary of making derogatory remarks about certain winemaking methods (i.e. rotary fermenters). These comments can show a lack of understanding of the wine industry as a whole and can 'make the Examiners blood heat up!' (to quote one Examiner).

penalty_signals.signal: Premium-only framing
penalty_signals.quote: Candidates must not just focus on the premium end of the market…

examples_expected.specificity: The question-specific commentary sets no example granularity; the Paper 2 preamble governs — examples must support the argument, be global, and cover all wine types where appropriate.
examples_expected.quote: Examples should be used to support arguments/statements rather than as statements of fact. Examples should also be global and cover all wine types where appropriate.

scope_traps.trap: Drifting into viticulture and harvest decisions rather than vinification
scope_traps.quote: The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process. A brief mention of harvesting grapes at optimum phenolic ripeness is fine but candidates must focus on the winemaking.

scope_traps.trap: Treating tannin management as a premium-wine concern only
scope_traps.quote: it could be argued that judicial tannin management is more important at "entry level" - pressing off skins before the end of primary fermentation is common practice.

performance_note: "This question had the highest pass rate in the Paper."
extraction_notes: examples_expected.quote is taken from the Paper 2 preamble, not from this question's own commentary, because the question-specific commentary does not discuss examples — a grader should weight the example requirement here as paper-wide rather than question-specific.

question_text: Discuss the impact of malolactic fermentation, or its absence, on wine style.
command_word_demand: "This question is looking for the candidate to give a concise definition of what malolactic fermentation is and does, and then apply this to a number of wine styles outlining the relevant impact that MLF has on that style." The examiners stress this needed planning, not the default Paper 2 process narrative: "this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers."

definitions_required.quote: This question is looking for the candidate to give a concise definition of what malolactic fermentation is and does, and then apply this to a number of wine styles…

definitions_required.term: the bacteria responsible for MLF (Oenococcus oeni)
definitions_required.quote: The main cause of concern was a failure to define clearly the bacteria responsible for malolactic fermentation.

required_elements.element: Give a concise, watertight definition of MLF and what it does, up front
required_elements.quote: With this in mind, students were likely to run into trouble later in the paper if their introduction wasn't watertight.

required_elements.element: Name the bacteria correctly and currently — Oenococcus oeni, not Leuconostoc oenos — and know it occurs naturally
required_elements.quote: It was previously called Leuconostoc oenos but the name was changed in the late 1990's and therefore scripts should be clear in referencing the current name… In addition several students seem convinced that Oenococcus oeni doesn't occur naturally - perhaps due to the fact that winemakers do add it as a cultured bacterium.

required_elements.element: Demonstrate the full process — bacteria involved, fermentation temperature, possible risks — and tie each to style impact
required_elements.quote: Candidates must demonstrate a thorough understanding of the MLF process - bacteria involved, fermentation temperature, possible risks - and discuss this in relation to the impact on wine style (acid reduction, bi-products of the MLF).

required_elements.element: Apply MLF across styles with examples — sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified
required_elements.quote: It is important to give examples across styles from sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified to substantiate the argument.

required_elements.element: Discuss red wine properly, including reds that do NOT undergo MLF
required_elements.quote: Too many candidates simply dismissed the impact of MLF on red wine as 'all red wines go through MLF'… the impact of MLF on red wines as well as reds that don't go through MLF could have had a paragraph of discussion. Apart from Nouveau styles, there are a number of sweet red wines on the market now that do not undergo MLF.

required_elements.element: Get the basic science right — direction of pH change, realistic MLF temperatures
required_elements.quote: The main issue however seemed to be technical misunderstandings. Not only were the bacteria involved a confusion for candidates but also the basic science of MLF. pH levels were all over the place and either rose or fell after MLF. Ideal temperatures to conduct MLF also varied from ''low 12ºC'' to "high 36ºC".

required_elements.element: Structure by wine category plus non-style impacts
required_elements.quote: The best looked to break it down into red wines, white wines/sparkling bases and other impacts such as microbiological.

credit_signals.signal: A planned structure splitting reds / whites and sparkling bases / other impacts such as microbiological
credit_signals.quote: It also required careful planning - this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers. The best looked to break it down into red wines, white wines/sparkling bases and other impacts such as microbiological.

credit_signals.signal: Recognising where the marks actually lay — whites and sparkling
credit_signals.quote: Clearly, there were more marks to be gained in considering the impacts on white and sparkling wines…

penalty_signals.signal: Failing to define the bacteria responsible, or using the superseded name
penalty_signals.quote: The main cause of concern was a failure to define clearly the bacteria responsible for malolactic fermentation. Students need to update their knowledge of LAB strains.

penalty_signals.signal: Claiming Oenococcus oeni does not occur naturally
penalty_signals.quote: In addition several students seem convinced that Oenococcus oeni doesn't occur naturally…

penalty_signals.signal: Dismissing reds with 'all red wines go through MLF'
penalty_signals.quote: Too many candidates simply dismissed the impact of MLF on red wine as 'all red wines go through MLF'.

penalty_signals.signal: Answering almost entirely on Chardonnay
penalty_signals.quote: More importantly a number of candidates attempted the question centred almost exclusively on the impact of MLF on Chardonnay with a brief mention of aromatic white wines and thus didn't answer the question with sufficient breadth.

penalty_signals.signal: Wrong or inconsistent technical facts on pH movement and MLF temperature
penalty_signals.quote: pH levels were all over the place and either rose or fell after MLF. Ideal temperatures to conduct MLF also varied from ''low 12ºC'' to "high 36ºC".

penalty_signals.signal: Defaulting to the winemaking flow-chart template
penalty_signals.quote: this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers.

examples_expected.specificity: Spread across sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified — breadth of style, not depth on one variety.
named_in_report: sweet red wines on the market now that do not undergo MLF
examples_expected.quote: It is important to give examples across styles from sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified to substantiate the argument.

scope_traps.trap: Reading the question as being about Chardonnay
scope_traps.quote: a number of candidates attempted the question centred almost exclusively on the impact of MLF on Chardonnay with a brief mention of aromatic white wines and thus didn't answer the question with sufficient breadth.

scope_traps.trap: Ignoring the 'or its absence' half of the stem
scope_traps.quote: the impact of MLF on red wines as well as reds that don't go through MLF could have had a paragraph of discussion.

performance_note: "Perhaps because this question seemed fairly straightforward at first glance, a great many candidates chose it. Only one really gave an excellent and comprehensive answer along with a few passable ones. The rest seemed to struggle."
extraction_notes: The report itself supplies substantive technical content on Oenococcus oeni (acid tolerance, 10% ethanol tolerance, the Leuconostoc oenos renaming) — this is examiner text, not extractor knowledge, and is quoted as such. Note the doubled apostrophes in ''low 12ºC'' are as printed in the source.

question_text: What are the winemaker's options and challenges in colour management for different wine styles?
command_word: What are the winemaker's options and challenges
command_word_demand: A two-part stem, and the examiners marked papers down for answering only the first: "a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only." Breadth with restraint was the demand: "With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example."

required_elements.element: Answer both parts — options AND challenges
required_elements.quote: Most candidates seemed comfortable covering colour extraction techniques in different winemaking styles, but a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only.

required_elements.element: Establish the core relationship between colour and skins across a wide variety of process options
required_elements.quote: A broad essay inviting the candidate to demonstrate their knowledge of a wide variety of process options and the core relationship between colour and skins.

required_elements.element: Treat the inter-related questions of tannin management, pH and wine stability
required_elements.quote: The inter-related notions of tannin management and also pH and wine stability are critical.

required_elements.element: Address spoilage: rot-related colour destabilization and oxidation, deliberate or accidental, post fermentation
required_elements.quote: Spoilage factors from rot- related colour destabilization through to oxidation - deliberate or accidental - post fermentation should also have been addressed.

required_elements.element: Cover post-fermentation processes, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak), fining and the role of oxygen
required_elements.quote: Candidates also often failed to mention, or showed poor understanding of, winemaking processes post-fermentation, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak) and fining, as well as the role of oxygen. The best answers covered at least a few of these areas, giving a much more complete answer to the question.

required_elements.element: Open with a clear, well-structured introduction that maps the answer
required_elements.quote: As with all large, open questions where there is the temptation to write too much, a good, clear introduction is necessary. A well-structured introduction lays out the map for answering the question - candidates who have one generally stand a good chance of passing.

required_elements.element: Give specific, factual detail rather than vague comparatives
required_elements.quote: Others used statements like "high temperatures" and "longer time" - more specific, factual insight was required.

credit_signals.signal: Using the chronology of the winemaking process as the structural spine
credit_signals.quote: Paper 2 answers generally benefit from using the natural structure and chronology of the winemaking process as a basis for their structure - for the Examiner it is logical and easy to follow and shows an organised pattern of thinking. It also helps the candidate identify areas of interest that might easily be forgotten under the pressure of the Exam.

credit_signals.signal: Covering at least several of the neglected post-fermentation areas
credit_signals.quote: The best answers covered at least a few of these areas, giving a much more complete answer to the question.

credit_signals.signal: Good tempo and logical flow, with technical assumptions never in doubt
credit_signals.quote: Passing answers normally have a good tempo and a logical flow - and the Examiner should of course never be questioning a candidate's technical knowledge or assumptions about winemaking practices.

penalty_signals.signal: Describing colour extraction only — first half of the question answered
penalty_signals.quote: a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only.

penalty_signals.signal: Vague, unquantified statements
penalty_signals.quote: Others used statements like "high temperatures" and "longer time" - more specific, factual insight was required.

penalty_signals.signal: Silence on, or poor understanding of, post-fermentation processes, additions, fining and oxygen
penalty_signals.quote: Candidates also often failed to mention, or showed poor understanding of, winemaking processes post-fermentation, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak) and fining, as well as the role of oxygen.

penalty_signals.signal: Getting bogged down in one winemaker's practice at the expense of coverage
penalty_signals.quote: With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example.

examples_expected.specificity: Used with a light touch to illustrate a point — the report explicitly warns against extended description of a single producer's practice. The Paper 2 preamble adds that examples should be global, cover all wine types where appropriate, and support arguments rather than stand as statements of fact.
examples_expected.quote: With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as colour extraction (i.e. red winemaking) only, rather than colour management across different wine styles
scope_traps.quote: Most candidates seemed comfortable covering colour extraction techniques in different winemaking styles, but a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only.

performance_note: "Despite being a large topic area with many different areas to address, this should have been a relatively straightforward question to approach." No attempt or pass rate is stated for this question.
extraction_notes: A large share of this commentary is Paper 2-wide essay craft advice (introductions, chronological structure, tempo) that the Panel Chair applies generically; it has been recorded but a grader should not treat structure alone as the discriminator. A page number ('the natural structure and 12 chronology') was removed from one quote.

question_text: Examine the pros and cons of skin contact during the winemaking process.
command_word_demand: The examiners want a declared method of attack and genuine analysis, not enumeration: "Although the question seems straightforward, it is very important to clarify how it will be approached… The question can thus be approached either through each category of wine or by the various outcomes that will be affected by skin contact." And: "Time and again the one thing that appears lacking is evidence of original thinking, or critical analysis."

definitions_required.quote: Candidates must provide a useful definition of skin contact and should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified).

required_elements.element: Provide a useful definition of skin contact
required_elements.quote: Candidates must provide a useful definition of skin contact…

required_elements.element: Cover red, white and rosé, and all wine styles — table, sparkling and fortified
required_elements.quote: should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified).

required_elements.element: Do not exclude red winemaking on the grounds that all reds have skin contact
required_elements.quote: While it can be useful to clearly state the areas you will address in your answer it is not acceptable to state that you will omit areas like red winemaking because all red wines have skin contact.

required_elements.element: Show good understanding of the processes for each wine colour and style, supported by examples from around the world
required_elements.quote: Candidates should demonstrate a good understanding of the processes involved with each wine colour and style and use examples from around the world to support their statements.

required_elements.element: Choose and declare a coherent approach — by wine category or by outcome
required_elements.quote: The question can thus be approached either through each category of wine or by the various outcomes that will be affected by skin contact.

required_elements.element: Cover both sides: the range of skin contact methods AND their risks
required_elements.quote: Such answers showed understanding as well as knowledge, covering a range of skin contact methods and their risks.

required_elements.element: Reach summary-level concepts — e.g. that all wines have some element of skin contact, or the ten-year trend to more extraction on whites and less on reds
required_elements.quote: Good (but all too few) answers to this question broached summary concepts, for instance that all wines experience an element of skin contact, or that there has been a trend in the past 10 years to aim for more extraction on whites and less extraction on reds.

required_elements.element: Use examples to show multiple routes to one outcome, or one technique serving different outcomes
required_elements.quote: Few candidates are able to present examples in a way that shows there are different ways to the same solution (e.g. winemaker 1 does A to arrive at C, while winemaker 2 does B to arrive at C) or that one can use the same techniques to arrive at different outcomes (e.g. winemaker 1 punches down because they like gentle tannin extraction, while winemaker 2 punches down to achieve full extraction).

credit_signals.signal: Demonstrating that the wine world is complex, local and global at once, and changing
credit_signals.quote: In this way the candidate can demonstrate that the world of wine is complex and subjective, highly localised and global, and ever changing - and that they understand it.

credit_signals.signal: Detailed but economical prose
credit_signals.quote: Good, passing answers are detailed but do not waste words or repeat them.

credit_signals.signal: Broaching summary concepts and trends rather than only mechanisms
credit_signals.quote: Good (but all too few) answers to this question broached summary concepts, for instance that all wines experience an element of skin contact, or that there has been a trend in the past 10 years to aim for more extraction on whites and less extraction on reds.

penalty_signals.signal: Poor structure or an incomplete answer that omits major winemaking styles
penalty_signals.quote: As per the previous question, failure often resulted because of poor structure or incomplete answers that failed to address major winemaking styles (red, rosé, white etc).

penalty_signals.signal: Listing everything known about the topic as a substitute for an answer
penalty_signals.quote: There is definitely a trend for candidates to list all they know about a topic area as a form of answer - this will rarely pass, or producing a load of examples with no context or argument linking them.

penalty_signals.signal: An introduction that only announces the essay and restates the question
penalty_signals.quote: A number of introductions end with sentences like, 'This essay will examine…' and then repeat the question, failing to refer the Examiner to what the candidate intends to write and conveys a lack of mastery or flow on the topic.

penalty_signals.signal: Announcing that red winemaking will be skipped
penalty_signals.quote: it is not acceptable to state that you will omit areas like red winemaking because all red wines have skin contact.

examples_expected.specificity: Global, and deployed comparatively — showing different routes to the same outcome, or the same technique serving different outcomes — rather than listed without context.
examples_expected.quote: Candidates should demonstrate a good understanding of the processes involved with each wine colour and style and use examples from around the world to support their statements.

scope_traps.trap: Narrowing the question to white/orange 'skin contact' wines and skipping red and rosé
scope_traps.quote: should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified).

performance_note: "A similar style question to the previous one, answered perhaps slightly better with a handful of good passes. Also quite similar to a question from last year's Exam so perhaps candidates were well prepared for this very topical area."
extraction_notes: The commentary names no producers, regions or wines, so named_in_report is empty despite examples being explicitly required. The 'winemaker 1 / winemaker 2' passage is an examiner illustration of METHOD, not a factual example to be reproduced.

question_text: What are the most common causes of bacterial spoilage in wine? What effect do they each have, and what measures can be employed to guard against them? Your answer may consider the whole grape growing and winemaking process.
command_word: What are the most common causes … What effect do they each have … what measures can be employed
command_word_demand: A three-part enumeration that had to name the actual bacterial spoilage organisms and cover roughly half the ground on each: "Acetobacter and LAB were the main issues to be covered here but several candidates failed to mention LAB and thus could not gain good marks if ignoring approximately half the required coverage."

definitions_required.quote: A definition of "spoilage" would have been useful here as too many talked about general microbial issues in the vineyards and wasted time rather than focusing on the negative effect on the wine itself.

required_elements.element: Cover both Acetobacter and lactic acid bacteria (LAB) — omitting LAB forfeits roughly half the marks
required_elements.quote: Acetobacter and LAB were the main issues to be covered here but several candidates failed to mention LAB and thus could not gain good marks if ignoring approximately half the required coverage.

required_elements.element: Confine the answer to bacteria — demonstrate the distinction between bacteria and fungi/yeast
required_elements.quote: However far too many candidates seemed unaware of the difference between bacteria and fungi (different kingdoms of life!) and wasted time talking about Brettanomyces and yeast.

required_elements.element: Supply technical and numerical detail rather than qualitative description
required_elements.quote: Some technical and numerical detail was essential here to gain good marks.

required_elements.element: Focus on the negative effect on the wine itself, not general vineyard microbiology
required_elements.quote: too many talked about general microbial issues in the vineyards and wasted time rather than focusing on the negative effect on the wine itself

credit_signals.signal: The question was fully answerable to a high standard — top scripts reached the high 70s
credit_signals.quote: A very varied standard of answers with marks ranging from 20s to high 70s. This showed that the question could be answered well.

credit_signals.signal: Cite actual technical values rather than vague comparatives (paper-level expectation for Paper 3)
credit_signals.quote: Vague comments like "lower levels of SO2" are not sufficient - actual numbers are required.

penalty_signals.signal: Spent time on Brettanomyces and yeast, which are not bacteria
penalty_signals.quote: far too many candidates seemed unaware of the difference between bacteria and fungi (different kingdoms of life!) and wasted time talking about Brettanomyces and yeast

penalty_signals.signal: Classified TCA, reduction, mildew or botrytis as bacterial problems
penalty_signals.quote: Some even believed that TCA, reduction, mildew and botrytis were bacterial issues.

penalty_signals.signal: Failed to mention LAB at all

question_text: What are the principal pests and diseases facing vine growers today, and how can they best be managed?
command_word: What are... and how can they best be managed
command_word_demand: Critical to answering well was defining 'principal', 'pests and diseases', and 'manage', then triaging to a focused set (examiners suggest 7-8) of globally important pests/diseases with clear management/control arguments, rather than an unfocused catalogue.

definitions_required.quote: Critical to answering it well was defining 'principal', 'pests and diseases', and 'manage'.
Critical to answering it well was defining 'principal', 'pests and diseases', and 'manage'.
Critical to answering it well was defining 'principal', 'pests and diseases', and 'manage'.

required_elements.element: Triage to a focused set of 'principal' pests/diseases (examiners note candidates had scope to focus on 7-8) rather than an unfocused list
required_elements.quote: Examiners are aware of the sheer number of issues affecting vine-growers globally, and thus set a broad range of pests and diseases that could be considered, giving candidates the opportunity to focus on 7-8 of which they considered important.

required_elements.element: Distinguish physical pests (e.g. deer) from pests that transmit disease (nematodes, leafhoppers, mites, mealybugs)
required_elements.quote: Good passing papers considered the differences between physical pests such as deer, and those pests transmitting diseases: nematodes, leafhoppers, mites, mealybugs.

required_elements.element: Discuss and distinguish key bacterial/fungal diseases (Pierce's Disease, Flavescence Dorée, botrytis, Eutypa, Esca) from viral ones (fan leaf virus, red blotch, leafroll)
required_elements.quote: Likewise, it was critical to discuss (and distinguish) between key bacterial/fungal diseases such as Pierce's Disease, Flavescence Dorée, botrytis, Eutypa, Esca, and viral ones such as fan leaf virus, red blotch and leafroll.

required_elements.element: Present arguments and examples demonstrating understanding of managing and controlling each disease/pest discussed
required_elements.quote: The key to a pass here was clearly presenting arguments and examples demonstrating an understanding of managing and controlling the said disease.

required_elements.element: Consider varying growing conditions and producer philosophy, discussing management options for organic/biodynamic growers as well as conventional growers
required_elements.quote: Discussions of management needed to consider varying growing conditions and the philosophy of the producer; the best papers confidently discussed management options open to organic/biodynamic growers as well as the less restrictive ones available to more conventional growers.

credit_signals.signal: Highlighted real experience from direct knowledge of producers and demonstrated global awareness
credit_signals.quote: This was a question in which the best papers clearly highlighted the writer's real experience due to direct knowledge from producers, and demonstrated their global awareness of the situation.

credit_signals.signal: A detailed, well-organised answer peppered with relevant examples, defining 'principle'/selection criteria, considering costs and biodynamic/organic treatments
credit_signals.quote: A very detailed answer, well organised and peppered with relevant examples. It defined 'principle' or how the pests/diseases discussed were selected, considers costs and considered biodynamic/organic treatments as well. It mentioned most of the pests and diseases, and detailed how they could be curtailed.

credit_signals.signal: Kept the discussion of phylloxera short and noted it is no longer a significant threat in most places due to better knowledge
credit_signals.quote: Many papers (not all!) nominated phylloxera as (still) a principal pest. So long as the discussion of management was relatively short and pointed out that it is not a significant threat in most places due to better knowledge, examiners were positive in their marking consideration.

examples_expected.specificity: named specific pests/diseases (deer, nematodes, leafhoppers, mites, mealybugs, Pierce's Disease, Flavescence Dorée, botrytis, Eutypa, Esca, fan leaf virus, red blotch, leafroll) rather than generic treatment
examples_expected.quote: Good passing papers considered the differences between physical pests such as deer, and those pests transmitting diseases: nematodes, leafhoppers, mites, mealybugs.

scope_traps.trap: Not triaging to focus on the 'principal' pests/diseases, risking 'not see the wood for the trees'
scope_traps.quote: If one didn't do some form of triage and focus on those that are 'principal' around the world today, and knowing what to do about them, it was very easy to "not see the wood for the trees".

performance_note: A popular question and the most successfully answered overall.

question_text: "This wine has been bottled un-fined and unfiltered." Assess the implications for the winemaker.
command_word_demand: Tested knowledge of what procedures are available, what is legal in different parts of the world, the difference between fining and filtration, and — crucially — what other winery activities can be undertaken, or are implied, if fining and filtration are forsaken.

definitions_required.term: fining and filtration (the difference between them)
definitions_required.quote: Confusion over the difference between fining and filtration was also quite surprising - candidates must have clear definitions of these two processes before starting a question such as this.

required_elements.element: Address what procedures are available and what is legal in different parts of the world
required_elements.quote: A question that tested candidates' knowledge of what procedures are available, what is legal in different parts of the world, what the difference is between fining and filtration (which wasn't always clearly addressed!) and - crucially - what other winery activities can be undertaken, or are implied, if fining and filtration are forsaken.

required_elements.element: Discuss how yields, sulphur dioxide regime and vat/barrel ageing might be deployed to achieve greater stability and clarity in the absence of fining and filtering
required_elements.quote: The major over-riding omission was the simple failure to talk about how things like yields, sulphur dioxide regime and vat/barrel ageing might be deployed to achieve greater stability and clarity in the absence of fining and filtering.

required_elements.element: Look at the whole range of winemaking procedures that can be employed to eliminate the need for fining and filtration
required_elements.quote: The more successful responses to this question looked at the whole range of winemaking procedures that can be employed to eliminate the need for fining and filtration.

required_elements.element: Take a technical approach to the implications for the winemaker, not a list of who is doing what
required_elements.quote: It also seemed difficult for students to discuss the implications for the winemaker of making unfined and unfiltered wine. A list of who is doing what, as opposed to a technical approach, is not enough.

penalty_signals.signal: Preferred to consider labelling and marketing implications of 'bad winemaking' rather than the technicalities of winemaking
penalty_signals.quote: Quite a few candidates preferred to consider the labelling and marketing implications of what might be considered bad winemaking rather than the technicalities of winemaking, which is what this paper is about.

penalty_signals.signal: Gave a list of who does what rather than a technical approach
penalty_signals.quote: A list of who is doing what, as opposed to a technical approach, is not enough.

penalty_signals.signal: Confused fining and filtration
penalty_signals.quote: Confusion over the difference between fining and filtration was also quite surprising - candidates must have clear definitions of these two processes before starting a question such as this.

scope_traps.trap: Discussing labelling/marketing implications of unfined and unfiltered wine rather than the technical winemaking implications
scope_traps.quote: Quite a few candidates preferred to consider the labelling and marketing implications of what might be considered bad winemaking rather than the technicalities of winemaking, which is what this paper is about.

extraction_notes: Paper 2 preamble reinforces this as a technical, not marketing, paper: "Paper 2 is a technical paper and you cannot pass without including technical details!" and warns against "who does what where" answers lacking critical thinking.

question_text: Sauvignon Blanc appears in many styles throughout the world. Compare and contrast Sauvignon Blanc winemaking practices around the world.
command_word_demand: Examiners were looking for discussion of reductive versus oxidative winemaking, use of expressive yeasts, use of oak, international examples and blending, backed by sound technical information, across both premium and high-volume production.

required_elements.element: Discuss reductive versus oxidative winemaking, use of expressive yeasts, use of oak, international examples and blending
required_elements.quote: Examiners were looking for a discussion of reductive versus oxidative winemaking, use of expressive yeasts, use of oak, international examples and blending.

required_elements.element: Back up comments with sound technical information
required_elements.quote: The candidates needed to back up their comments with sound technical information.

required_elements.element: Cover high volume wines, not just high quality/terroir-driven wines
required_elements.quote: Some less well prepared candidates tended to waffle and focus almost solely on high quality, terroir-driven wines while neglecting the presence of high volume wines.

required_elements.element: Use international examples to support reasoning, beyond a narrow set of familiar producers/styles
required_elements.quote: This question gave the candidates the opportunity to demonstrate their reasoning with use of international examples to support their arguments. Few took this opportunity.

credit_signals.signal: Showed good knowledge and understanding of why wines differ from the same variety, and that a winemaker can embrace many options with knowledge, skill and courage to step away from a mainstream trend
credit_signals.quote: Some excellent responses to this question showed good knowledge and understanding and got to the essence of why wines are different from the same variety and how, with a variety such as Sauvignon Blanc, a winemaker can embrace a great many options if they have the knowledge, skill and the courage to step away from a mainstream trend.

credit_signals.signal: Gave welcome thought to technical winemaking such as separating press fractions, types of fining practices, use of residual sugar, and stabilisation
credit_signals.quote: A small number of essays gave welcome thought to technical winemaking such as separating press fractions, types of fining practices, how residual sugar may be employed, and stabilisation.

penalty_signals.signal: Overgeneralised, relying on very frequent reference to only a few examples, e.g. Fumé Blanc in the USA, without considering newer producers making complex Sauvignon Blanc there
penalty_signals.quote: The examiners commented on the very frequent reference to only a few examples, for example Fumé Blanc in the USA without considering newer producers who are making complex Sauvignon Blanc in that country.

penalty_signals.signal: Waffled and focused almost solely on high quality, terroir-driven wines, neglecting high volume wines
penalty_signals.quote: Some less well prepared candidates tended to waffle and focus almost solely on high quality, terroir-driven wines while neglecting the presence of high volume wines.

examples_expected.specificity: international examples beyond a narrow, frequently-repeated set (e.g. beyond just Fumé Blanc USA), covering both premium and high-volume production
examples_expected.quote: The examiners commented on the very frequent reference to only a few examples, for example Fumé Blanc in the USA without considering newer producers who are making complex Sauvignon Blanc in that country.

scope_traps.trap: Overgeneralising Sauvignon Blanc winemaking to one or two familiar reference points (e.g. Fumé Blanc USA) instead of comparing and contrasting across the world
scope_traps.quote: Candidates should however beware of overgeneralisation.

question_text: Discuss the roles of enzymes in winemaking.
command_word_demand: Required starting from a definition of what an enzyme is and what it does, then working systematically through the winemaking process discussing enzyme use at each stage across red, white and rosé winemaking.

definitions_required.quote: Those candidates that did not do well failed to define what an enzyme is and what it does.

required_elements.element: Start at the beginning of the winemaking process and work through discussing the use of enzymes at the various steps and stages
required_elements.quote: Like so many other essays, candidates should have started at the beginning of the winemaking process and worked their way through discussing the use of enzymes at the various steps and stages.

required_elements.element: Discuss enzymes in red, white and rosé winemaking
required_elements.quote: Candidates needed to discuss red, white and rosé winemaking.

required_elements.element: Use a systematic approach covering the whole winemaking process as a structure to hang points on
required_elements.quote: Again, a systematic approach covering the whole winemaking process would allow candidates a structure on which to hang their points.

penalty_signals.signal: Rarely mentioned enzymes in red winemaking, demonstrating a big, general gap in knowledge
penalty_signals.quote: It was interesting to note how few candidates mentioned enzymes and red winemaking, demonstrating a big, general gap in knowledge.

penalty_signals.signal: Covered commercial enzyme types but few, if any, discussed spoilage enzymes present in grapes
penalty_signals.quote: Commercial enzyme types were mostly covered but few, if any, candidates discussed spoilage enzymes present in grapes.

performance_note: This was one of the less popular questions on this year's theory paper two. A competent candidate had the ability to really shine here and get high marks whereas less confident candidates found it extremely challenging — results were good passes or clear fails with very little in between.
extraction_notes: The corpus question text reads "Discuss the roles of enzymes in winemaking" (plural 'roles') while the report commentary restates it as "Discuss the role of enzymes in winemaking" (singular). Extraction follows the corpus wording per instructions; discrepancy noted.

question_text: Compare and contrast winemaking techniques best employed for Syrah grown in Cornas, McLaren Vale and Hawke's Bay.
command_word_demand: A 'micro-terroir' question requiring students to accurately describe what makes each named region distinct from other classic regions in its own category (e.g. McLaren Vale from Barossa, Cornas from other Rhone appellations), and to compare/contrast winemaking techniques across the three and how they impact quality and style — not treat each region as generically representative of its country/zone.

required_elements.element: Show a good understanding of winemaking in each of the three named regions (Cornas, McLaren Vale, Hawke's Bay)
required_elements.quote: This question required a good understanding of winemaking in the regions described.

required_elements.element: Accurately describe what makes McLaren Vale distinct from other classic Australian regions and what makes Cornas distinct from other classic Rhone appellations
required_elements.quote: it opened up into a far greater invitation to the student to accurately describe what makes McLaren Vale distinct from other classic Australian regions such as Barossa, and what makes Cornas distinct from other classic Rhone appellations.

required_elements.element: Compare and contrast the different winemaking techniques in the three regions and how they impact quality and style
required_elements.quote: This was a huge micro-terroir question, potentially allowing students to compare and contrast the different winemaking techniques in the three regions, and how they impact on quality and style.

penalty_signals.signal: Described McLaren Vale as if it were part of a gigantic generic Australian whole, and Cornas as if entirely representative of all Northern Rhone reds
penalty_signals.quote: Very few answers addressed this, with most electing to describe McLaren Vale as if it were part of a gigantic generic Australian whole and Cornas as if it were entirely representative of all Northern Rhone reds.

examples_expected.specificity: meso-region level distinction, e.g. McLaren Vale versus Barossa, Cornas versus other Rhone appellations, not treating a named region as generic for its country/zone
examples_expected.quote: it opened up into a far greater invitation to the student to accurately describe what makes McLaren Vale distinct from other classic Australian regions such as Barossa, and what makes Cornas distinct from other classic Rhone appellations.

scope_traps.trap: Treating this as a red-wine version of Question 2 (a generic variety comparison) instead of engaging with the specific micro-terroir/regional distinctions demanded
scope_traps.quote: At first this may have felt like a red wine version of Question 2. In fact, it opened up into a far greater invitation to the student to accurately describe what makes McLaren Vale distinct from other classic Australian regions such as Barossa, and what makes Cornas distinct from other classic Rhone appellations.

scope_traps.trap: Describing a named region as generically representative of its wider country/zone rather than addressing its distinctiveness
scope_traps.quote: Very few answers addressed this, with most electing to describe McLaren Vale as if it were part of a gigantic generic Australian whole and Cornas as if it were entirely representative of all Northern Rhone reds.

performance_note: Although few candidates attempted this question, many papers were competent with few really poor answers. Students mostly understood Rhone/Cornas winemaking, some were conversant with McLaren Vale/warm climate areas, but fewer were conversant with Hawke's Bay.

question_text: Temperature management is the key to modern winemaking. Discuss.
command_word_demand: A wide-ranging question needing to touch on temperature management across many aspects of winemaking — from fruit storage, processing, fermentation, through to long term storage — not fermentation temperature management alone, using specific temperature values and following the chronology of the winemaking process.

required_elements.element: Cover temperature management beyond fermentation — fruit storage, processing, fermentation, through to long term storage
required_elements.quote: Overall this was a wide-ranging question that needed to touch on many different aspects of winemaking - from fruit storage, processing, fermentation, through to long term storage. Very few candidates covered all these areas.

required_elements.element: Include specific temperature values, not just wide hedged ranges
required_elements.quote: On a question such as this, temperature values do need to be included. Either these were missed out or candidates hedged their bets with larger ranges: 10-16ºC.

required_elements.element: Employ the chronology of the winemaking process as a structure, considering the role of temperature management at each step
required_elements.quote: Better answers always employ the chronology of the winemaking process. Considering the entire winemaking process in a systematic manner and thinking about the role of temperature management at each step will ensure that no points are missed.

penalty_signals.signal: Focused on the temperature management of fermentation only, losing marks for not elucidating other areas where temperature management is important
penalty_signals.quote: The main issue with this widely-answered question was that many candidates tended to focus on the temperature management of fermentation only and thus lost marks by not elucidating other areas where temperature management is important.

penalty_signals.signal: Hedged bets with large temperature ranges (e.g. 10-16ºC) instead of precise values
penalty_signals.quote: Either these were missed out or candidates hedged their bets with larger ranges: 10-16ºC.

penalty_signals.signal: Lacked sound technical understanding of must chilling, and treated cold soaking on white and red wines as an equivalent term
penalty_signals.quote: Examiners commented on lack of sound technical understanding of must chilling. Cold soaking on white and red wines is not an equivalent term.

scope_traps.trap: Narrowing the question to fermentation temperature management alone rather than the whole winemaking process
scope_traps.quote: The main issue with this widely-answered question was that many candidates tended to focus on the temperature management of fermentation only and thus lost marks by not elucidating other areas where temperature management is important.

scope_traps.trap: Treating cold soaking as an equivalent term for white and red wines
scope_traps.quote: Cold soaking on white and red wines is not an equivalent term.

question_text: How, and to what extent, can yeast influence the final style and quality of wines?
command_word_demand: Not a request to write "Everything I know about yeast"; required naming specific yeast genus/species (correctly spelled) and analysing their influence on style and quality rather than generic or narrow-minded assertions.

required_elements.element: Name specific yeast species used in winemaking, not write an entire essay on yeast without mentioning a single species
required_elements.quote: Examiners also remarked on some candidates' ability to write an entire essay on yeast without once mentioning a single species.

required_elements.element: Know the names of common yeast types (good or bad) and spell them correctly
required_elements.quote: Paper 2 is a technical paper and not only do candidates need to know the names of common yeast types involved in the winemaking process (be they good or bad!) but they also need to be able to spell the names of the yeast correctly.

required_elements.element: Grasp the role of different yeast genus and species in influencing style/quality
required_elements.quote: Questions related to yeasts appear with some regularity so it is surprising to see candidates still failing to grasp the role of the different yeast genus and species.

required_elements.element: Use global and relevant examples
required_elements.quote: It is also wise to ensure the examples used are global and relevant.

credit_signals.signal: Kept up to date with current R&D on yeast (an area where much R&D is spent)
credit_signals.quote: This is one area where much R&D is spent so students would be wise to keep themselves up to date with what is going on.

penalty_signals.signal: Wrote an entire essay on yeast without once mentioning a single species
penalty_signals.quote: Examiners also remarked on some candidates' ability to write an entire essay on yeast without once mentioning a single species.

penalty_signals.signal: Made narrow-minded comments such as 'selected yeasts only produce short lived wines' or 'Spoilage yeasts and Brett can be used to bring out terroir', not suggesting deep understanding
penalty_signals.quote: Narrow minded comments such as "selected yeasts only produce short lived wines"... or "Spoilage yeasts and Brett can be used to bring out terroir"… do not suggest a deep understanding.

penalty_signals.signal: Made generalisations about old world and new world wine styles
penalty_signals.quote: Nor do generalisations about old world and new world wine styles.

examples_expected.specificity: global and relevant examples of yeast species/use
examples_expected.quote: It is also wise to ensure the examples used are global and relevant.

scope_traps.trap: Treating the question as an invitation to write everything known about yeast rather than addressing how and to what extent yeast influences style and quality
scope_traps.quote: This question was not asking for "Everything I know about yeast". We urge candidates to address the question and not just tell us everything they know about a particular topic.

question_text: Outline the most important quality control checks during bottling and why each is necessary.
command_word_demand: A lot of candidates missed the critical "why" part of the question, and without considering this, their answers were too superficial and lacked analytical depth.

required_elements.element: Consider quality checks on both the wine itself and on the packaging process/dry goods, plus compliance with product specification
required_elements.quote: Candidates needed to consider both quality checks on wine and checks on the packaging process and dry goods, as well as compliance with product specification.

required_elements.element: Explain why each check is necessary, not just describe the bottling process
required_elements.quote: Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question, showing lack of awareness of key QC analyses for wine and why they are carried out - essential knowledge for potential MWs.

required_elements.element: Consider a HACCP framework
required_elements.quote: Consideration of HACCP is always useful in a question that mentions bottling.

required_elements.element: Show awareness of EU legislation and ISO requirements as part of the quality assurance framework
required_elements.quote: Quality control is part of the overall quality assurance process and wine is a food stuff which must comply with legislative and regulatory standards (so an awareness of EU legislation and ISO requirements is helpful).

required_elements.element: Cover staff safety risks (broken glass, noise, heavy lifting, health exposure) and wine/business risks (quality loss, consumer disappointment, brand damage, recall costs)
required_elements.quote: The safety of staff handling the liquid and the packaging is critical (risks like broken glass, noise, heavy lifting and exposure to health risks). Issues for the wine itself include loss of quality, consumer disappointment, damage to brand, and costs attached to issuing recalls or being unable to sell the wine.

penalty_signals.signal: Lack of focus, missed too many key issues
penalty_signals.quote: There were few really strong answers to this question and lots of candidates lacked focus or missed too many key issues.

penalty_signals.signal: Described the bottling process rather than addressing quality control
penalty_signals.quote: Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question, showing lack of awareness of key QC analyses for wine and why they are carried out - essential knowledge for potential MWs.

penalty_signals.signal: Omitted the analytical "why"
penalty_signals.quote: A lot of candidates missed the critical "why" part of the question, and without considering this, their answers were too superficial and lacked analytical depth.

examples_expected.specificity: actual numbers (e.g. EU SO2 limits, pH values, additive usage levels, filtration pore sizes), not vague statements — a paper-wide expectation from the Chair's General Comments
examples_expected.quote: Vague comments like "lower levels of SO2" are not sufficient - actual numbers are required.

performance_note: There were few really strong answers to this question and lots of candidates lacked focus or missed too many key issues.
extraction_notes: The numeric-precision/examples expectation is drawn from the Paper 3 Chair's General Comments (paper-wide), not stated specifically for this question.

question_text: What analyses should be carried out at the winery pre- and post-bottling to ensure that a wine is in good condition and conforms to legal requirements for sale?
command_word: What analyses should be carried out
command_word_demand: Specifically, the question asked "what analyses" yet there were disappointingly few answers which listed and explained the key QC analyses and their importance in ensuring the wine's good condition and conformation to legal requirements.

required_elements.element: List and explain the key QC analyses required, not just discuss issues that might arise
required_elements.quote: Several candidates simply discussed issues that might arise and not what QC checks were required.

required_elements.element: Know legal limits (EU or other key markets) for key wine constituents, additives, and allergens
required_elements.quote: Candidates also needed to know legal limits (EU or other key markets) for key wine constituents and additives, plus allergens.

required_elements.element: Know labelling requirements (e.g. sweetness declarations, allergens, sulphite declarations, alcohol tolerances)
required_elements.quote: Knowledge of labelling requirements was also required (e.g. sweetness declarations such as medium-dry or halbtrocken, allergens, sulphite declarations, alcohol tolerances).

required_elements.element: Support the answer with supporting examples
required_elements.quote: Supporting examples would be helpful too.

penalty_signals.signal: Overall lack of technical information and analytical reasoning
penalty_signals.quote: Here again the key problem was the overall lack of technical information and analytical reasoning in many of the answers.

penalty_signals.signal: Answers judged "too qualitative"
penalty_signals.quote: The comment "too qualitative" was used by examiners for many of the scripts.

examples_expected.quote: Supporting examples would be helpful too.

scope_traps.trap: Discussing potential wine faults/issues that might arise instead of naming the QC analyses required
scope_traps.quote: Several candidates simply discussed issues that might arise and not what QC checks were required.

performance_note: This question had the highest pass rate at 50%, indicating that it was straightforward for candidates with good levels of technical knowledge.

question_text: Many winemakers are reducing the levels of free and total sulphites in wine. Consider the role of sulphites at bottling and until the wine reaches the end consumer. What are the implications of reduced levels of free sulphites?
command_word_demand: The "implications" part of the question required a definition of what "reduced levels" of free SO2 mean.

definitions_required.quote: The "implications" part of the question required a definition of what "reduced levels" of free SO2 mean.

required_elements.element: Cover the four properties of SO2: anti-oxidant, anti-microbial, anti-oxidasic, and (less important) binding with acetaldehyde
required_elements.quote: The four distinct properties of SO2 - anti-oxidant, anti-microbial, anti-oxidasic and (less important) binding with acetaldehyde.

required_elements.element: Know current EU levels for total SO2, typical levels of free SO2 in different wine styles, and what constitutes "lower levels" in actual numbers
required_elements.quote: It is still surprising how many candidates do not know current EU levels for total SO2, nor typical levels of free SO2 in different styles of wine, nor what constitutes lower levels in actual numbers. It is really important to have these facts committed to memory.

required_elements.element: Be clear about the difference between free and total SO2
required_elements.quote: Clarity about the difference between free and total SO2 is also important.

required_elements.element: Address both parts of the question directly: the role of sulphites, and the implications of reduced free SO2 levels
required_elements.quote: There were, however, lots of very good scripts which did address (both parts of) the question directly and met the standard to pass.

credit_signals.signal: Addressed both parts of the question directly (role of sulphites AND implications of reduced free SO2)
credit_signals.quote: There were, however, lots of very good scripts which did address (both parts of) the question directly and met the standard to pass.

penalty_signals.signal: Rolled out a pre-prepared essay on the use of SO2 with disregard for the exam question's focus

penalty_signals.signal: Did not know current EU/typical SO2 numeric levels
penalty_signals.quote: It is still surprising how many candidates do not know current EU levels for total SO2, nor typical levels of free SO2 in different styles of wine, nor what constitutes lower levels in actual numbers.

examples_expected.specificity: actual numeric facts — current EU total SO2 levels, typical free SO2 levels by wine style, and what "lower levels" means in real numbers
examples_expected.quote: It is still surprising how many candidates do not know current EU levels for total SO2, nor typical levels of free SO2 in different styles of wine, nor what constitutes lower levels in actual numbers. It is really important to have these facts committed to memory.

scope_traps.trap: Answering as if the question asked how to reduce sulphites / achieve low-sulphite winemaking (a Paper 2-style question), rather than the implications of already-reduced free SO2 levels
scope_traps.quote: instead of addressing the "implications of reduced levels of free sulphites", they wrote about the implications for the winemaker of reducing free sulphites/how to achieve low sulphite wines. Their essays thus focused on adjustments to be made in the winemaking process, so treating it substantially as a Paper 2 question.

question_text:
Briefly discuss three of the following showing their importance to the handling of wine:

a) Preservatives in wine
b) Preventing deposits in bottled wine
c) Inert storage
d) Pre-bottling filtration
command_word_demand: Writing 'short notes' still has to evidence sufficient knowledge and understanding for MW level and use supporting examples. ... Those candidates who failed this question usually did so because their answers were insufficiently wide and/or deep in scope in addressing the chosen topic.

required_elements.element: Cover the chosen topic with sufficient breadth and depth for MW level and use supporting examples, not a narrow technical listing
required_elements.quote: Writing 'short notes' still has to evidence sufficient knowledge and understanding for MW level and use supporting examples.

question_text: Identify the most important trunk diseases in vineyards around the world. How can they be best controlled and managed?

command_word_demand: A two-part question where both parts had to be answered in depth: "Critical to success here was answering both parts of this question. Less successful papers did well on identifying the most important trunk diseases, but failed to consider in depth control and management."

required_elements.element: Answer both parts — identification AND control/management
required_elements.quote: Critical to success here was answering both parts of this question.

required_elements.quote: A passing paper had to include at least three of the four to five key diseases noted globally. Many papers discussed Esca and Eutypa, but left out Botryosphaeria and Phomopsis.

required_elements.element: Acknowledge the global reach of these diseases — regional differences, varietal susceptibility, differing treatments
required_elements.quote: Key to a successful answer was an acknowledgement of the global reach of these diseases: differences, varieties, treatments.

required_elements.element: Compare and contrast control techniques according to location and climate
required_elements.quote: Examiners commented that many papers simply didn't do an adequate job of comparing and contrasting various techniques to deal with these diseases depending on location and climate.

required_elements.quote: The best papers highlighted diseases affecting younger vines specifically, like Petri disease or black foot disease.

credit_signals.signal: Coverage of young-vine trunk diseases beyond the standard Esca/Eutypa pair
credit_signals.quote: The best papers highlighted diseases affecting younger vines specifically, like Petri disease or black foot disease.

penalty_signals.signal: Identifying diseases well but treating control and management superficially

question_text: Is the use of cover crops worthwhile in viticulture?
command_word_demand: An opinion question requiring a judgement of effectiveness, evidenced: "Perhaps because the question had a certain "Op-Ed" aspect, requiring a candidate to express an opinion (based upon sound factual examples and knowledge, however), this made for more fluid discussion." The analysis had to place cover crops in a wider viticultural context and judge them: "The question as set was asking for an analysis that looked at cover crops as one component of viticulture, perhaps in relation to climate change, or to the unique challenge of a particular terroir, but also considered the effectiveness of a given approach."

required_elements.element: Demonstrate what cover crops actually do, differentiated by climate and by water availability
required_elements.quote: This question demanded clear understanding of what cover crops do, in different climates, and depending on availability of water.

required_elements.element: Judge utility against intended purpose rather than listing where cover crops are or are not used
required_elements.quote: It was not enough to list examples of where cover crops are used or not; it was necessary to discuss their utility … in the context of their intended purpose.

required_elements.element: Address both advantages and disadvantages, with examples showing where they are 'worthwhile'
required_elements.quote: Advantages and disadvantages needed to be addressed, and examples used to demonstrate where the use of cover crops may be considered 'worthwhile'.

required_elements.element: Develop four to six positive or negative reasons, each properly discussed
required_elements.quote: Good candidates used four to six positive or negative reasons, each discussed well.

required_elements.element: Site-specific nuance — slope, site vigour, frost potential, organic certification
required_elements.quote: Good answers were attuned to the particular uniqueness of various sites relative to slope, site vigor and frost potential or certification for organic viticulture.

required_elements.element: Economic utility — the extra cost of planting and cultivating cover crops relative to wine type and value
required_elements.quote: It was also useful to consider the economic utility of cover crops, considering the extra cost entailed in planting/cultivating cover crops relative to the wine type and value produced.

credit_signals.quote: Good papers noted more nuanced utility; for example, cover crops used to prevent erosion and help with water penetration in the harsh Douro climate.

credit_signals.signal: Framing cover crops as one component of a viticultural system, e.g. against climate change or a particular terroir challenge

penalty_signals.signal: Sweeping unqualified generalisations in place of evidenced opinion
